utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today is Tuesday, November 18th, 2008. Good morning to the Prosecution, Mr. Mundis and Mr. Dutertre. Good morning to everyone assisting us in this case. Good morning to Mr. Seselj. This week, we are going to have as our first witness Ms. Bilic, an expert witness. Then we'll have a lady who will testify about Hrtkovci, and we'll complete the week with Anna Maria Radic, our second expert witness. And with respect to this last witness, Anna Maria Radic, I have a number of questions to put to Mr. Seselj. I know that he has requested some time to deal with a number of issues today, and my question may be one of the questions he wanted to raise. With respect to Witness Radic, on the 16th of June, 2008, the Trial Chamber allowed the replacement of Ivan Grujic by Visnja Bilic and Anna Maria Radic as expert witnesses called by the Prosecution to testify in relation to exhumations and identification processes in Croatia and missing persons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 13th of November, 2008, the Trial Chamber, having allowed Visnja Bilic to be called as an expert to testify on the 18th of November, 2008, the accused stated that it would be ideal for both witnesses to testify one after the other: "It would be easier for me," he said, "to prepare myself for my cross-examination." Transcript page in French 11754. Anna Maria Radic's report and the relevant documents were disclosed to the accused in his own language on the 13th and 14th of November, 2008, by the Prosecution. On the 17th of November, 2008, the Prosecution disclosed Anna Maria Radic's report pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules and requested for this report and the relevant documents to be added to the 65 ter list. Unfortunately, because of time constraints, B/C/S translation of this motion has not as yet been given or submitted to the accused. Anna Maria Radic, being scheduled to testify on the 20th of November, 2008, and the times to respond having not -- not having been complied with, the Trial Chamber has the following questions to put to

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you challenge the additions to the 65 ter lists requested by the Prosecution? Secondly, do you accept the expert witness report of Anna Maria Radic? Thirdly, do you wish to cross-examine her? Fourthly, do you challenge the qualifications of Ms. Radic as an expert witness? And, finally, do you challenge the relevance of her report? Five questions in total, and I'm sure you can give us one response for these five questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps I misheard. At one point, I understood that the Prosecution had asked for the report of Anna Maria Radic to be introduced as 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not 92 bis. 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then, maybe I misunderstood something or the interpreter said something wrong. I can't be sure which. You know my permanent handicap caused by the administrative ban on communication with my associates, and it is still ongoing. This is a disruption which has grown into an objective disruption, and I believe it is not so great for me to ask a suspension of the proceedings. I'm coping quite well with Prosecution witnesses, even without the cooperation of anyone from the outside world, outside the prison and outside the courtroom. Of course, in the dilemma between the quality of defence in case 1 and case 2, the prevailing factor for me is the expedience of the trial with a high-quality defence or slowing down of the trial with super-quality defence. It would be better, of course, for me to have communication with my advisers. But the report of Anna Maria Radic was given to me, was given to me last Friday; and I have nothing against her continuing as a Prosecution witness. I challenge the addition of new 65 ter documents, according to the motion of the Prosecution, but that's because I challenge and dispute all Prosecution motions. In this case, I have no particular reason to challenge this evidence proffered by the Prosecution. I would challenge evidence of good weather if they submitted it. I challenged the expertise of Anna Maria Radic, and I will prove that she is not qualified. I do not accept her report. And there again I come across a very serious problem. The report has no title, just as Visnja Bilic's report has no title. Neither you nor I know the topic of their respective reports. It's all a bit hazy. Certain questions were asked of them, as in a quiz. They answered these questions, but there is no subject of the expert report. We have never come across such a case again. Every expert report had a certain topic, a subject. These two have none. Two women sat down and wrote down what they wanted to write.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me interrupt you, Mr. Seselj. If you will look at the documents we have and the documents you have, we find a letter by Ms. Dahl. Ms. Dahl is not here today, but Mr. Mundis can speak on her behalf. And Ms. Dahl wrote to the expert witness and requested or, rather, asked a whole series of questions and requested very specific answers. If you look at this letter, you will realise that it's the outline of the report of the expert witness. I'm sure you've received Ms. Dahl's letter in your language, because it must have been translated, and I would encourage you to read through all the questions raised by Ms. Dahl and put by Ms. Dahl to the expert witness, asking her to provide answers to these questions. I wanted to point that out to you, when I hear you say that you do not quite see what the point of the expert witness report is. But later on Mr. Dutertre will put questions to the expert witness, and as part of the cross-examination you'll be able to deal with all this. The Judges will put questions, so we'll be able to explore all this very thoroughly. Let me give back the floor to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, everything is crystal clear to me. I do not challenge that these two expert reports have a skeleton. I understand the questions asked by Christine Dahl of Anna Marie Bilic [as interpreted]. There is no title in my view. An expert report first of all has to have a title. There has to be a topic of an expert report, and the topic has to be set out in the title. That is missing. Abd that's what I wanted to point out. The skeleton does exist. What kind of skeleton, we'll see in cross-examination. Furthermore, I told you already I reject both reports, including the Anna Maria Radic report. I insist to cross-examine her. I challenged the relevance of her report, and one of the administrative issues I had announced is this: I am astounded that only half an hour has been given me to cross-examine an expert, Anna Maria Bilic [as interpreted]. I need much more time. We are dealing with an expert. How can I question an expert in half an hour? Of course I'll demonstrate that she's not an expert, but until I've proven that, she stands here as an expert, and of course I need more time. And speaking of experts, expert reports are proffered into evidence as a whole, and the Prosecution does not need as much time as Defence does. The Defence needs much more time, especially since I had no opportunity to respond to her expert report, as I had the opportunity with Oberschall or Theunens or some others. In those cases, I had engaged my own experts, who assisted me in preparing my response to these expert reports. So I need more than half an hour. I don't know how much you envisaged for Anna Maria Radic. I'll need more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me consult my fellow Judges about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After considering the matter, the Trial Chamber rules that the Prosecutor will have three-quarters of an hour to put questions to the witness. The Trial Chamber takes note of the fact that we have a report, we have related documents, and that the Prosecutor will be able, within 45 minutes, to present the report and to highlight a number of key documents. As for you, Mr. Seselj, you will have an hour and a half, one hour and a half, to cross-examine the witness. The Trial Chamber would like to remind you that we have already heard evidence about exhumations, about all the steps taken to identify the victims. Therefore, this expert report is in line with other evidence we've heard in this trial. Within this hour and a half, thus, we believe you will have ample time to cross-examine the witness, even more so that on Thursday we'll have another witness who will talk about a related subject. I believe that in an hour and a half, you will have all the time necessary to put your questions, knowing that the Judges will also put questions to the witness. I, myself, have a very relevant question to put to the witness. I can immediately tell you what it is so that you'll be able to prepare yourself. When reading this report, I realised that in Croatia, there were several detention centres and various sites where bodies were exhumed. Therefore, we have many more victims than only the victims found at Ovcara. And based on this question of mine, the witness may be able to provide information I would like to have and that I find missing about the scope and the total number of victims and identified bodies. That's why this witness is so relevant. Yes, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning. Good morning to Mr. Seselj. Let me make a few comments. First of all, the report was submitted to Mr. Seselj a long time ago. If he wanted to make written submissions, he would have the time to do so. Secondly, the report has not as yet been admitted into evidence. It's up to the Prosecution to put questions to the witness and ask for its submissions. Thirdly, what is important is what questions the witness answered to in her report. With respect of the time allocated to Mr. Seselj, it's up to the Chamber to decide. Then with respect to the detention centre and exhumation sites, we have called the witness to talk to us about the armed conflict and the victims, and that's why we are going to -- we've called this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm satisfied with the hour and a half you've given me. That will be enough, and I hope I will get as much to cross-examine Anna Maria Radic. I wanted to raise another issue regarding these administrative problems. The Prosecution again submitted to me a revised sequence of Prosecution witnesses through end of December. Some new names appear here, and I have to protest that for Witness VS-1007, the Prosecution envisaged his testifying under 92 ter. I don't know what has been confirmed, that the witness will come or that he will testify under 92 ter. All I know is that a year ago, you decided that this witness should appear viva voce. And I still insist on his testifying viva voce, because he was a prominent political figure during the war, and especially today he's a prominent political figure in one of the states that resulted from the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, and it would be really scandalous for that person to just come in and out of the courtroom under 92 ter, whereas I believe that such an important political figure has to testify publicly in full. That's Witness 1007, and out of an abundance of caution I will not mention his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall consider the matter. I had no idea that VS-1007 was such a relevant and prominent personality. We'll review the decision we took, a decision where we decided which witnesses would testify viva voce and which witnesses we decide pursuant to 92 ter. You state that we decided that that witness should testify viva voce. You're saying that the Prosecution is challenging this decision. Since the witness is not coming tomorrow, we'll have a few days to re-explore the matter. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Dr. Seselj, and everyone in and around the courtroom. On the 11th of November, 2008, the Prosecution filed a 92 ter motion with respect to Witness VS-1007. This was based upon the Trial Chamber's decision of 7 January 2008 concerning a number of statements which the Prosecution proposed to tender in written form. With respect to VS-1007, in its decision of 7 January 2008, the Trial Chamber did deny that application for 92 ter with respect to this witness. However, he was among the category of witnesses for which the Trial Chamber specifically allowed the Prosecution to reapply, and that is what we have done as of the 11th of November, 2008; that is, last week. We have reapplied pursuant to the Trial Chamber's specific authorisation allowing us to do that in its decision of 7 January 2008. I would expect and hope that CLSS would be making a translation of that motion available to the accused so that he can respond to that in writing, but I will indicate that a motion has been filed pursuant to the Trial Chamber's decision of 7 January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I told you earlier, the Trial Chamber will consider this motion and the relevant statement, based on the factors used by the Trial Chamber. When a witness challenges a the conduct of the accused, fairness dictates that the accused should be able to cross-examine the witness. And since Mr. Seselj has decided not to cross-examine 92 ter witnesses, we have to be extremely cautious in that respect, because our guiding light in this Chamber is to establish the truth, and that's what we should be all working for, to establish the truth. So I'm going to review this statement extremely carefully, and we'll either decide to maintain our decision as it is or to hear the witness viva voce. But it will all depend, of course, on the statement, and I don't have the statement in front of me because I had no idea the matter would be raised this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would now like to tell you something important, but first of all you should insist that the Prosecutor inform you whether this witness is planned as a protected witness and whether he enjoys any protective measures, because I was not explicitly informed on that issue. I only know that he is listed under a code name, a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no idea. Are there specific measures with respect to that witness? I don't have his details in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Nor do I at this moment, Mr. President. Perhaps if I could make a suggestion. I would anticipate that during the course of this week, there will be some time available for us to discuss this matter or any other pending matters. We do have a witness who's waiting to testify, and with all due respect I would suggest that we commence with that. Again, with three witnesses scheduled this week, I do anticipate we'll have some time, perhaps tomorrow or even Thursday, that we could address this or any other matter that the accused would like to raise. But I would respectfully suggest that we get on with the witness that's scheduled for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right, Mr. Mundis. We are going to hear the witness now. I always have my file in front of me, and I can tell you that with respect to VS-107 [as interpreted], no protective measures have been requested. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for being so conscientious and having all the information handy, the information that the Prosecutor doesn't. I can say it's Sulejman Tihic, who is the successor of Alija Izetbegovic as president of the SDA party. He is a key political figure for Bosniak Muslims today; and such a key figure should not appear under 92 ter, with the Prosecution compiling his statement and that statement going directly into evidence. The Prosecution would have not put him on the witness list were he not important. Since he is on the witness list, he is a very important witness to me, and that's why I insist that Sulejman Tihic testify viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have noted your submissions. We are going to review the matter, and we'll let you know what we decide very shortly. Don't worry about this. Let's now have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Could you please state your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Visnja Bilic. I was born on the 20th of December --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness. There is a lot of paper shuffling in the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a professor of psychology by occupation, but currently I'm working as head of department in the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons at the Ministry for Inter-generational Solidarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your date of birth has not been properly recorded. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20th November 1966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, have you already testified before a national or an international tribunal about the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or is this a first for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never before testified before a court of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. What you have just said has been recorded. Please read out the solemn declaration. The usher is going to show you the solemn declaration, and I would like you to read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let give you some information about the way we are going to proceed today. You've just stated that you've never testified before, and this is probably something you will remember for the rest of your life. I would like to give you all the necessary information about the way we are going to proceed for your testimony to run as smoothly as possible. You've probably met with the Prosecutor already. Later on, he will put questions to you. You've met him as part of the preparation of your testimony. The Prosecutor will put questions to you and show you a number of documents. This is a classical or typical phase of testimony that usually runs extremely smoothly. It may happen that the Judges put a number of questions to you themselves, based on the questions put to you by the Prosecutor or based on the documents. When the Judges put questions to the witness, there's usually no problem. Now, a tricky stage of the testimony is usually the cross-examination. Mr. Seselj happens to be representing himself. As a result, he will be putting questions to you himself. Let it be very clear for you. Mr. Seselj is entitled to challenge your credibility. He's entitled to put questions about your qualifications. Some of the questions may be a bit disturbing, a bit embarrassing, but that's the way it goes during a cross-examination. The accused is also entitled to deal with matters of substance based on his case, on his Defence case; and he will most probably, because he told us he will do so, he will most probably challenge the substance, the content of your report. Following that, the Prosecution will, if he decides to do so, put additional questions to you. That's the way we're going to proceed for your testimony. Rest assured that the Judges are always in control, including during cross-examination, and if one or the other parties oversteps the mark, the Judges are here to intervene and to call every man back to order. We are dealing with the concept of exhumations, identification of victims. It's very technical subject matter and should not give rise to diatribes and speeches, because we're dealing here with a very technical topic. And since we are dealing with such a topic, please try to be extremely specific when you answer the questions. If you to not understand the question, ask for the question to be rephrased, even if the person asking the question is a Judge. We have breaks every 90 minutes. We started this morning at 8.30. The first break, therefore, will happen at 10.00 a.m., in one hour time. And we have 20-minute breaks. Of course, the Trial Chamber is always ready to listen to you. If at any point in time you feel unwell, raise your hand immediately and we'll adjourn for a little while to allow you to rest. I think I've covered everything. Mr. Dutertre, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apologies. I was on the wrong channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have 45 minutes to go through your report, Mrs. Bilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Shall I repeat what I said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mrs. Bilic, we have 45 minutes to go through your report and the appendix, and please make very short and very brief answers, very concise answers. You will shed light on the question of detained persons and missing persons who were gone missing during the conflict in Croatia between 1991 and 1995. And you will also be giving your insight on the means that were implemented to find them again. This aspect, of course, is very -- of great importance to the Judges, who will have to rule on the Ovcara massacre. There are two binders that are on your right. One is labelled in blue, blue print and marked with a "1," and the other one has a red print label and is marked with a "2." And to make it easier to know which binder I'm talking about, I'll ask you to refer to document X in the red binder or document Y in the blue binder. In these binders, you will find a number of documents that can be identified with a number, and in our jargon here we call it the 65 ter number. So this being said, let me move to a few general questions, Ms. Bilic, first on your resume and also on the Administration for Missing Persons, the administration in charge of the matters we are interested in today. A very short question to start with, could you please tell us what is the present name of the Croat state entities who today deal with people that went missing during the conflict in Croatia between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: That is the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons of the Ministry for Family, War Veterans and Inter-generational Solidarity, as a body performing professional and administrative affairs linked to the tracing of missing persons. And the other body is the Administration of the government -- the Commission of the Government of Croatia Detainees and Missing Persons as an independent government body of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now take a look at the first document in the blue binder, binder number 1, and look at document 7278 in the 65 ter list. Ms. Bilic, is this your resume?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Three short questions. You answered a question from the Presiding Judge, saying that you were head of the administrative department in the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons. I'd like to know exactly when you started working within this organisation in charge of detainees and missing persons.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. If I read your resume correctly, you were appointed at the head of the Department for Detainees and Missing Persons in 1995. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So if my math is right, you've been dealing with this issue for 15 years. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender this resume. And since she's already been qualified as an expert, I will not go into this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, to speed things up, you might -- you should maybe do the tendering at the end of your examination, rather than having this ping-pong game where we ask the Registrar for a number and then have the number, and so forth and so on. It would be faster to tender everything at one time after your examination. Just say, "I would like to tender documents such-and-such and such-and-such" at the end of your examination. That way, if need be, Mr. Seselj can raise a comprehensive objection. Otherwise, he may raise objections for each document, and we will waste a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if there's a global objection, unfortunately it's very imprecise, and then we have to re-discuss every document one after another. But if you want me to work this way, I will make a global tendering at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On your resume, I have a question, Ms. Witness. In 1991, you got a psychology diploma. It's a social psychology degree. So could you please tell us how psychology studies are going to have a link with missing persons? Could you give us the link?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, I started working in what was then the Office of the Government of Croatia for the Victims of War as an adviser and a psychologist in the Department for Missing Persons. However, as this was a state administration, as time went by, I became an employee in that body, that is to say, the state administration; and that is how I began working in the field of detainees and missing persons further afield as a broader investigation, not just a psychologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, at first, at the very beginning in 1991, could you tell us the name given by the Croat administrative authorities to this organisation that had been set up to deal with missing persons?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: In 1991, in the Republic of Croatia, the following were founded: Two commissions, in fact, dealing with the question of detainees and missing persons. One was the Commission for Handling Persons Detained in Armed Conflicts in the Republic of Croatia, and the second was the Commission for Tracing Persons Missing in Combat Actions in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. So if I understand, organisations were set up extremely quickly. Now, could you give us an approximative number, approximative, I repeat, of administrative changes this organisation in charge of tracing missing persons went through between 1991 and 2008? I would just like to have the figure, because we have the whole history in your report. I would just like a ballpark figure right now.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Now, despite all these administrative changes, I mean, we know this is important, but can you tell us whether, despite all these changes, the information -- the archives that had been collected were always transferred to the successive organisation, whatever their name at the time?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There is continuity with respect to the archives, and the archive is transferred or was transferred from one body to another, that is to say, bodies in charge of dealing with detainees and missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Your answer, as I heard it through the French translation, you said that archives were transferred to a second organisation. Is this a translation problem or do you mean that this was a transfer to all organisations, one after the other? Could you please shed some light on this?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the bodies took over -- or, rather, every time a new body was established for detainees and missing persons, on the basis of the provision of the government of Croatia, would take over the archive from the previous bodies that dealt with issues of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And was it more or less the same people working in all these different organisations?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same people, so that the archive was managed by the same people and that there was continuity there, and that's what the case is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So we have understood that archives were transferred. And could you tell us whether you had the same access to this information as Mr. Grujic would have?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you be more specific when you say "mostly"?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: What I meant was the following: Certain documents within an archive, or the archive that we have at our disposal, are classified by degrees of confidentiality. Now, if those documents were not relevant for my work, then I didn't have an insight into those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Then I would like to ask you a follow-up question. Did you have access to all the documents you needed in order to draft your report?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And this is going to bring us to the report, quite naturally. Could you please take a look at the document before last in the red binder, not the binder you have but the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Before you go to this document, I have a question for you. The Prosecutor talked about Mr. Ivan Grujic. We know that Mr. Seselj was challenging something in this area. The Trial Chamber does not have all the elements at its disposal. Unfortunately, we sort of have to go fishing for information, and sometimes -- and sometimes witnesses prove very useful in that respect. So as far as you know, have you heard -- have you heard about the fact that Mr. Grujic would have been challenged in his work, challenged according to the work he was doing? Either you were aware of this and you say, "Yes," or you're not and you answer just answer by, "No."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't hear of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well. If you'd answered with a "yes," I would have went on with my questions. But since you were negative, I will now give the floor back to Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, could you please move -- could you please take a look at the red binder, binder number 2, and find document at the -- the document before last in this document, which is number 7413 in the 65 ter list. This is my question, if you have the document now: Do you recognise this document as the letter that the OTP wrote to you on July 11th, 2008, to commission a report on the issue of detained and missing persons in the conflict in Croatia between 1991 and 1995, more specifically, regarding the issue of the Ovcara exhumation? In the singular, "exhumation." What is the title we should give to this document? The title requested by Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I didn't understand what the title could be, what the Prosecutor said, the title of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is very marginal as an issue, but the report on the -- report on the missing persons and detainees in Croatia in 1991 to 1995 with more information on Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's find a solution to this. If you had to give a title to your report, the report you were asked to -- you wrote after Ms. Dahl's letter on July 11th, 2008, what title would you have given to this report, because in your report you gave Ms. Dahl a great number of answers to all her questions, but what would be the overall title you could give to this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The process for tracing detainees and missing persons in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you please now take a look at the next document in the red binder, 7414 in the 65 ter list. Is this the report you sent to the OTP following the letter you received from the OTP on July 11th, 2008?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you please go to the last page of this document in the B/C/S version, and tell me whether you recognise your signature at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether the information in this report corresponds to a direct and personal knowledge you may have on the issue of detained and missing persons?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And could you tell us whether you were physically there during the Ovcara exhumation?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present during the exhumation at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Then in order to draft this report, did you use documents that had been drafted within your office, within your administration?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How long did it take you to collect all this information and draft the report?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, I needed roughly three weeks. Roughly three weeks is what I needed to compile my report and to update it with all the data and information that the report contains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will tender this document at the very end of my examination, but now let me turn to the way in which you collected information on missing persons. Could you please take a look at the blue binder, the first one, and take a look at the 12th document called 7357 in the 65 ter list. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you quickly tell the Judges how you used this document? What was the point of this document?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: This document is used for the collection of information on missing persons, persons who went missing during the war in Croatia, and at the end of 199 -- [B/C/S/ on English channel]. It was developed with a view to seeking information in the tracing process for each individual person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The document was drafted at the initiative of the then Commission for Detainees and Missing Persons by professionals from different areas of expertise: criminologists, forensic experts, psychologists, and persons versed in informatics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who is supposed to fill this document?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Educated personnel in the Red Cross of Croatia for tracing missing persons, on the basis of requests for tracing missing persons submitted by the relatives and family of the missing persons, and that is the signature you will find -- or, rather, that is what the signatures at the end of the document indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. So Red Cross members meet with relatives or family members and fill out the questionnaire with the help of these people; is that it?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: In 1994, an action was put into place, an organised action, for collecting up all the requests for tracing missing persons, and this was announced through the media, calling upon all families with missing family members that went missing connected with the war to report to the Croatian Red Cross and to table a request for tracing those persons, and these questionnaires were filled in at that time relating to the missing persons concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. This is very clear, and all this is explained in paragraph 7 of your report. There's one important point, as far as the issues that the Judges will have to rule upon. Could you please tell us what was so important in this form to have questions on the age, the nationality and the status of the people, be it civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Data about age were fairly important, and this was seen through the process of identification subsequently itself. Now, facts about nationality and other affiliation helped us in the tracing process. However, this information is based on the statements we receive from the family members, so they do not necessarily correspond to the actual state of affairs, the status as was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: This is clear. Thank you. Could you tell us why you had to include questions on this form that had to deal with the civilian or military status of these missing people? What was the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, as I was saying, it's important to know this fact because it can influence the tracing process and the identification of the mortal remains. It can prove essential in the subsequent process of identifying the mortal remains of a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. And it's on the basis of these questionnaires that you drafted the list of missing persons, but could you provide us with some more details about this particular process?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Correct. Based on these questionnaires -- well, first of all, they were computerised, so in addition to this hard copy, they exist in an electronic version. And based on the information provided in these questionnaires, a description of the missing persons was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where have all these questionnaires been archived?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The archives of the Department for Detainees and Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. We've covered the issue of the collection of information and the way the list of missing persons was drafted. Now let me move on to the issue of exhumations. You provide detailed explanation about this at paragraphs 8 to 14 of your report. We know that you were physically present at Ovcara when the exhumation took place, and I would like you to tell the Trial Chamber more specifically what role you played, practically speaking, during these exhumations on the ground.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify? I would be very grateful. Do you mean during exhumations in general or during the exhumation at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In general, what role do you play when you attend an exhumation? Are you just present as an observer? Do you take an active part in the process? What is the actual nature of your role?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: For the most part, I had contact with the families of victims that were supposed to have remains possibly in the site of the exhumations, but also other participants in the exhumation process. The purpose, therefore, was to collect information with a view to future identification of human remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you attended all the exhumations that occurred on the territory of Croatia to find missing persons or did you attend only part of these exhumations?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I attended one part of the exhumations conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. I would like you to turn, in the blue binder, the one you have in front of you, to turn to the 15th document, the document marked 65 ter number 7360. Ms. Bilic, this document is entitled "Overview of Exhumations in Counties." I have the following question to put to you: Who drafted this map and this table, where we have the number of bodies exhumed by county?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: That was drafted at the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons, the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you specify whether we are talking here about exhumations that took place following the conflict and in order to find people who went missing during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Correct. These were exhumations conducted in order to find the persons who went missing in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In what region was the highest number of bodies exhumed?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: In the area of the Vukovar-Srem county.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us, and that's to be found at the bottom of the document, what is the total number of bodies exhumed in Croatia, and what is the total number of bodies identified amongst these exhumed bodies?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Of exhumed remains at the time of the making of this report was 3.684, and out of these, 3.100 were identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. And this is for what particular date?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The 1st of July, 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a very relevant question to put to you, based on this document. It's a question that needs to be put. I read through your report, through all the annexes of your report, and something struck me. At paragraph 35 of your report, you stated that 2.796 war prisoners and civilians were detained in Vukovar, and exchanged and released. Thanks to this, we discover that in the Vukovar region, about 2.800 people were not killed, but were exchanged. And according to what you're saying, they had been detained in 11 detention camps. In the indictment, mention is made of 200 persons from the Vukovar Hospital who were killed, and the majority of whom were identified. When reading this portion of your report, I realised that these 200 individuals make up 10 per cent of the total number of people captured in Vukovar. But I also realised something else, based on your report. I realised that in the overall region of Vukovar, 2.017 persons were exhumed and 1.726 were identified; and there may be other mass graves that have not been identified as yet, so figures might be even higher. You told the Prosecutor that you attended the exhumation at Ovcara, where in that grave of seven by nine metres, 200 bodies were found. Based on these figures that are supported by documentary evidence, can you tell us, as of today, November 2008, can you tell us whether all the victims have been listed so far or are there victims who have not been listed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the victims, all the missing persons for whom families submitted requests for a search, have been recorded according to standards established by the ICRC. Also recorded were all exhumed and identified persons from mass and individual graves discovered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following evidence we've heard in this courtroom, and after having heard Mr. Seselj's defence case, I'm trying to understand why this precise number of 200 persons were killed at Ovcara. I'm trying to find an explanation with respect to that figure of 200 people, because we know that 7 persons were spared and that 200 were killed. Is it just by chance that this happened or does this number, this figure of 200, correspond to something very specific? Based on this question of mine and based on your report, I found that 184 Serbs - I don't think I'm mistaken - exactly 184 Serbs were killed on the territory of the Croatian Republic. Witness, out of these --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about these 184 recorded Serb victims? Is it the definite figure or were there more Serb victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the report, I cited the ethnicity, that is, the ethnic composition of persons who have been identified to date. Among the persons identified to date and exhumed in the area of Croatia, 184 were Serbs. Before the finalisation of the identification process, we cannot talk with any certainty about the ethnicity of persons who have been identified. At this moment, these are the exact figures, 184 identified Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There might be a problem with the transcript. [In English] ... persons who have been identified or not been identified. [Interpretation] Could we ask Ms. Bilic to specify -- to clarify what she just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about these 184 Serbs? Are these Serbs who went missing and who were later identified, or are these missing Serbs who so far have not yet been identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are persons who have been identified, whose families confirmed the identification, received the remains, and buried them as they wished. They were in contact with the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons. For them, the process of search is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that your administration and all Croatian departments of the state have regular contacts with their Serb counterparts. I suppose that as part of the reconciliation process, you have regular contacts, there are regular contacts between Serbia and Croatia. To your knowledge, what is the figure given by the Serb authorities, the figure of missing Serbs? Is it a figure provided by Serb authorities? Do they, for example, say, "Well, you're telling us that 184 Serbs were victims, but there were more than that"? Is there a dialogue, exchanges between Serbia and Croatia, with respect to that particular issue or is that something that is not raised at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Serbia, which was the FRY, relations were established under the agreement on missing persons in 1995. Since that time, there has been an exchange of information, documentation, and data that can help identification, but that is behind us. As for Serbian demands, the Republic of Serbia put up requests for around 400 citizens of the Republic of Serbia who they claimed went missing in the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see that I was right to put this question to you. You've just told us that as of today, the Republic of Serbia is looking for 400 citizens of the Republic of Serbia who, according to them, went missing on the territory of Croatia. This is, indeed, a very relevant piece of information. Let me go back to Vukovar now. This is my last question. In the indictment, mention is made of what happened after the fall of Vukovar, when civilian or military persons were transferred to Ovcara and where 200 people died. Thanks to your report, I discovered something I was not aware of up until yesterday. I discovered that 2.017 individuals died in the Vukovar region. This piece of information may prove to be relevant as well. I assume that you studied these 2.017 people killed, the 1.726 people identified. What about the bodies that were exhumed, these 2.017 bodies; what is the number of graves -- of mass graves these bodies were exhumed from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the exhumations of remains in the territory of Croatia and all identifications are performed in cooperation and with the coordination of the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons. Specifically, the identification of 2.017 persons in the Vukovar-Srem county were of people found in two [as interpreted] large mass graves and a large number of smaller graves.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 52 large mass graves and a large number of small graves, of which I cannot tell you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just stated that there were 52 large mass graves and a large number of small graves, where 2.017 persons were found. I may be mistaken, but in your report I did not see a map related to Vukovar-Srem and the exact locations of these 52 mass graves. Was this done, because I couldn't find any information in that respect in the documents we have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been made. I hope it's part of the documentation. It's very difficult for me to deal with these binders, but that map exists, it has been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 70 -- or document 7369 on the 65 ter list in the first binder. You won't find the 52 mass graves, but you will find the major graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In document 7369, we have a list of sites, various sites, and as just stated by Mr. Dutertre, we don't have 52 sites, we have about 20 of them, 20 at the most. But I was wondering, Witness, whether these 52 mass graves were located far away from Vukovar or not. If they are close to Vukovar, we could conclude that the victims hailed from Vukovar. But if the mass graves are further away, these people may be victims of other events. To your knowledge, were these 52 graves close or far away from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This map, this specific map, relates to mass graves where human remains of the victims from Vukovar were found. It's not a map of all the mass graves discovered in the area of the Vuk March-Srem county. It's a map of the 14 mass graves in the area of both Vukovar-Srem and Osijek-Baranja counties, where victims from Vukovar were found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's continue to look at this map we have in front of us. Here we have 14 graves. We have a grave at Ovcara identified here. We have Negoslavci and other sites. And what we can see here is some of the graves are located several dozens of kilometres away from Vukovar. To your knowledge, the victims who were exhumed at Ilok, were they killed on the spot or were they killed in Vukovar, to be then buried in Ilok? Can you provide an answer to that type of question or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the attachment to my report, there are lists of persons from Vukovar who have been identified, regardless of the location of the mass or individual grave where they were found, so these are persons who had gone missing or forcibly taken away from Vukovar. In case of any doubt, with the help of the documentation available to the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons, it was established that these persons were killed on the banks of the Danube, thrown into the river, and then their remains were recovered in the area of Ilok as still unidentified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The victims found at Ilok had been thrown into the Danube River, and they were found in the Ilok region and buried there. This is the gist of your answer. Let me now take the two sites we have at the top of the map. It's quite difficult to make out, but I believe that the one at the top is Dalj, Balj, something like that, and underneath that, sorry for the pronunciation, we have something that sounds or reads like Farma Lovas. Where did the victims come from, those thirty-two were buried on those two sites.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Victims found in Lovas farm and in the mass grave in Dalj were people detained in Borovo Komerc on 19 November 1991. Borovo settlement is an integral part of Vukovar town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How far away is Vukovar from Dalj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell you exactly. Perhaps ten kilometres. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, about ten kilometres. You have five minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean five minutes left for my direct examination? I hope not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, five minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 7362, 7362, a document you will find in the blue binder, and a document we've just discussed and thanks to which we were given very relevant additional information. It's a document entitled [In English] "Exhumed and identified mortal remains."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned this document at paragraph 32 of your own report. I have the following question to put to you: Who drafted this document, Ms. Bilic?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The document was made in the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons, where I work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you confirm that it was updated on the 1st of July, 2008?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Correct, I can confirm that. It was updated on the 1st of July, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Please turn to page 8 of the document in English. For you, it's page ERN number 0642-8287 in B/C/S, page 8 in English, including the cover page. Let me repeat the ERN number, 0642-8287. Could you confirm that when it was possible to establish the nationality of the exhumed and identified bodies, that 87 per cent of them were Croats? Is that the way we should understand the document?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Out of those identified, 87 per cent are of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please now turn to ERN number page 0642-8284, page 5 in English of the same document, page 5 in English, in the English translation of the document. Based on this document, can you confirm that 39 per cent of the persons identified were over 60?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Correct, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And to conclude, let's move to the previous page in English. In your language, ERN 0642-8283. Could you please tell us, what is the percentage of women amongst identified bodies?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The percentage of women among identified human remains is 28 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What is your view, generally speaking, on the impact of this conflict on the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The fact is that this data showed that a large percentage of victims were persons who were especially protected by the Geneva Conventions and their additional protocol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the question put by the Prosecutor is of paramount importance. If he had not put it to you, I would have put it to you; and Mr. Seselj may have asked you the same as well. Out of these 3.100 victims, we see that 30 per cent were female, 850 of them. This is rather a striking figure in such a conflict. How come the number of females killed was so high? Talking about these killed or identified females, can you tell us whether they belonged to the 18 to 60-year age group or whether they are over 60.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation ][Previous translation continues] ... report. This report does not show such detailed information about age with respect to sex, so I can't really say with any certitude. However, most of the women were women who were elderly, that is to say, persons who, before the war, had not left their homes. So they're mostly women who stayed on in their own homes and, unfortunately, fell casualty that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we compare these figures with the figures from the Vukovar Hospital, where two women were identified at the Vukovar Hospital, we're not talking about 30 per cent there, two females, then it seems a bit illogical. How come we have only two women who were killed at Vukovar, whether -- there should have been more of them, according to this percentage of 30 per cent. Can you provide us with some sort of explanation or is it something that you can't explain at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only two women were killed in Vukovar. Only two women were found in the mass grave at Ovcara. However, at the new cemetery, Novo Groblje in Vukovar, another mass grave on the territory of Vukovar, a large number of women were found; and I think that the share of women found in the area of the Vukovar and Srem county was equal to the total share of women shown in this Powerpoint presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is very interesting. Why is it that out of the group of people led from the hospital to Ovcara, there were only two women, only two? Do you have an explanation for this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Vukovar Hospital, and taken from the Vukovar Hospital, persons were forcibly taken away or went missing, they were people who were in the Vukovar Hospital at that time, who happened to be there at that moment, at least most of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in a hospital, you can very well expect to find a lot of women. There were children there, children who had been wounded, women who had been wounded because of the shelling, women who came to see their husbands who had been wounded as well. I know that when you study psychology, you also study statistics; and when you look at the statistics related to Vukovar, you find a lot of people -- a lot of women present at the hospital in Vukovar, many more so than at Ovcara. This is maybe something that has escaped everybody's attention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at all events, your question is a very interesting one. Now, the fact that it was mostly men who were taken away from the Vukovar Hospital can mean that they were subjected to the possibility of wounding more than women at that point in time, because the women were mostly in shelters and in facilities like that; whereas the men went to war, they engaged in warfare, they were members of the armed forces. So that very fact means that there was greater probability of the men being wounded than the women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. I believe it's time for the break, Mr. Dutertre, so we will have a 20-minute break. I believe you have some 20 minutes left, but Mr. Registrar will keep track of this for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Prosecutor, you have used up 32 minutes up until now, so if my math is right, you have 13 minutes left. Secondly, regarding Witness Anna Maria Radic, the Trial Chamber will issue a written decision, because motivation is quite extensive. However, I will read the disposition. So on these grounds, grants the Prosecution's motions and requests that Anna Maria Radic be heard before this Trial Chamber as an expert witness on November 20th, 2008; secondly, that the examination-in-chief last no more than 45 minutes; thirdly, that the cross-examination last no more than an hour and 30 minutes; and, fourthly, the Prosecution can add to its 65 ter list Anna Maria Radic's report and all relevant documents. Then, finally, the Trial Chamber states that it will rule on the admission of the said report and its relevant documents after having heard Anna Maria Radic's testimony. This is about Anna Maria Radic's testimony, but there will be a written decision that will be filed today. But because it's an emergency, I read the disposition. Now you have the floor, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, we know that the exhumation at Ovcara occurred in September 1996. Could you tell us why it didn't happen earlier?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The mass grave at Ovcara was in an area which was temporarily occupied and, thus, not accessible to the authorities of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know whether this site was surveilled or controlled by anyone before this exhumation?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the site of the mass grave at Ovcara was under the supervision and surveillance of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us what nationalities were the people who actually conducted the exhumation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The exhumation of the mass grave at Ovcara, on the basis of a request made by the International Court, was conducted by the international humanitarian organisation Doctors for Human Rights, which in this specific case was led by Dr. Snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that in French I heard "the International Court of Justice." I don't know if it's the exact translation. It said "the International Court," but I believe she was talking about this Tribunal. I'll ask for some details.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you're talking about International Court, you're talking about this court here?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said the International Criminal Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: That's another thing. ICTY, I guess.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether Serbian observers were present during the Ovcara exhumation?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The exhumation at Ovcara, during the time when I attended it as observer, had the status of observer, also present were Serbs, local Serbs, that is to say, of the occupied Croatian area of Podunavlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. How many bodies were exhumed in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The mortal remains of 200 persons were exhumed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And how many were identified?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: 193 persons were positively identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please look at the blue binder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question. I thought that Mr. Dutertre was going to put it to you, but he didn't. There was some Serbian observers. Fine. Could you tell us whether there were Croat observers? I mean, I'm not talking about you. You came from Zagreb. But local Croats, were they also there? For example, from the Vukovar municipality, maybe former Croats who used to live in the Vukovar municipality, or Croats that would have lived in the Croat Krajina in Croatia, those, you know, belonging to Mr. Goran Hadzic's movement. Were they present, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Access to the exhumation site at the mass grave at Ovcara was strictly restricted; so at the site itself, at the site of mortal remains, there were no representatives of local Croat authorities. However, there were representatives of local Serbs from the area, and they -- or, rather, the two of them were designated as observers during the exhumation process of the mass grave at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To your knowledge, why is it that no one found it useful to ask for Croat observers to attend, you know, local Croats? Why was it that there were only Serbs and no Croats? If you have an answer, of course. You might not have one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The local Croats at that point in time and in that area were not numerous, and especially not in the structures of power and authority. Most of the Croats in 1996 -- when the exhumation took place of the mass grave at Ovcara, most of the graves from that area were expelled and were in parts of the Republic of Croatia that were not occupied, not under occupation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But they could have been asked to come over, since some of them were in the Republic of Croatia. They could have been asked to come over. It wouldn't have been a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of an agreement between the government of the Republic of Croatia and the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, the OTP of the Tribunal, it was determined that from the Republic of Croatia, the process of exhumation of the mass grave at Ovcara would be attended by four observers, representatives of the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons, and experts and physicians, specialists in forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you see, when we put questions, we get answers. This was in the framework of an agreement between the OTP and the Republic of Croatia, and it's in this framework that all this was organised. And Judges didn't have their say in this, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Bilic, I would be interested to know a little bit more about the role of the Serb observers. They were locals; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct, they were local Serbs. That's what I said. In the situations when I attended the exhumation process, it was the representatives of local Serbs who were present, or, rather, their authorities, the Serb authorities, designated them as being observers of the process of exhumation that took place in the mass graves at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what exactly was their role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had the status of observers. I don't know what their role actually was. However, they did not have an active role in the process of exhumation itself of the mass grave at Ovcara. Their status was that of observer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would have thought that the Serbian authorities might be interested in appointing a forensic expert, or at least a medical doctor, or somebody who could verify the proper conduct of the exhumation, but there was nobody else appointed but these two gentlemen or persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that is something that I don't know about. I'm referring to two people, the two people who did attend during the period of time that I was there, that I attended as observer. So I don't actually know who was present and who was designated of the professionals by the Serb authorities to follow the exhumation process. It doesn't mean that there were no experts designated, but I'm saying that I don't know about that because while I was there, there was nobody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This is very helpful clarification. Last question: Did you see these two observers, the local Serbs, do anything or were they just hanging around the exhumation? Did they take photographs, or did they make notes, or did they talk to the experts, or what did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw them there while the exhumation process was in progress. They did not do any photographing. Nobody was allowed to take photographs. I really cannot remember now, since it's been 12 years since the event, whether on that occasion they communicated with the experts there who were conducting the exhumation or, rather, the representatives of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, whether they kept notes or anything like that. However, the documenting and recording of the process of the exhumation of the mass grave at Ovcara was not something that observers were allowed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With a previous expert witness, we saw some photographs, and we know that the mass graves had been guarded by the Russian army, who was there on behalf of an international mission. We saw that some tents had been erected. Now, you were there, I was not, so please tell us something. I assume that the bodies were exhumed, then were taken to the tents, and that the American forensic scientists, they were Americans with Dr. Snow, so that's when the American forensics performed the autopsies and did all the normal work done -- that is done in an exhumation. Is this the way it happened? The bodies were taken out of the grave, brought to the tent, and that's where the American forensic pathologists fill out their forms in performing their duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The American forensic experts were in charge -- well, not only American. I apologise. It was automatically that I said "American." That's not what I mean. The Doctors for Human Rights, that organisation, Physicians for Human Rights, was in charge of the whole process of the exhumation of the mass graves at Ovcara, taking out the mortal remains and so on, and the first preliminary examination of those mortal remains. They were in charge of that. Now, after that, the mortal remains were transported to Zagreb, to the Institute for Forensic Medicine and Criminology, attached to the Faculty of Medicine in Zagreb, where the experts, Physicians for Human Rights, in cooperation with professions and experts from the Institute for Forensic Pathology and Medicine, conducted the entire examination, the full examination of the mortal remains, the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would have been better for the on-site autopsies to be performed by these doctors from this human rights organisation, but also with the help of a Croat forensic pathologist as well as a Serbian forensic pathologist, so that there would be a panel of experts that could not be challenged. You know, experts that see the body, describe the body, photograph the body, and then determine the cause of death. Why was it not performed in such a way, as far as you know? Maybe it would be better to put these questions to the Prosecutor who was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is true, and it's a question that I can't give a proper answer to. However, the fact is that the conditions for dealing and processing the mortal remains were far better and more suited to the matter at the Institute for Crime Pathology and Forensic Pathology than at the exhumation site itself, but that was the plan. It was the OTP plan, and I can't really answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Dutertre, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, do you know who is Professor Delic, Dusan, of the Belgrade Forensic Institute?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I have no follow-up question, then. Could you please now take a look at document 7373 in the 65 ter list, in the blue binder, the first binder. The name of this document is the following: [In English] "List of identified persons whose remains were exhumed from the Ovcara mass grave. [Interpretation] It is a document referred to on page 36 of this report. Here is my question: Please tell us who made the list.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The list was compiled at the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons on the basis of official records of persons identified by this administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us who gave you these elements on the identification of these people?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: From the scientific and medical institution which conducted the process of identification for the mortal remains. In this specific case, it was the Institute for Forensic Medicine and Crime at the medical faculty at Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. When was this document updated for the last time?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of July, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where is the documentation that states the identification of all these people mentioned in this list?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: In conformity with the provision of the government of Croatia, the documentation is to be found in the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. After having looked at this list of 193 victims, I would like to move to the next document, number 7374 in the 65 ter list called, [In English] "Analysis of the annex 3 of the indictment." [Interpretation] You refer to this document in paragraph 37 of your report. First question, it's a simple and straightforward question: Who drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The document was compiled in the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: It was updated on July 1st, 2008; is that it?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Does this document give us information on all 265 victims that we can find in appendix 3 to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Correct, it is on the basis of appendix 3 to the indictment, referring to 265 victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now, I need your help to understand a few acronyms, and I believe that the Trial Chamber will also have the same problem if I don't clear this up. In the category column, we see an acronym, "D/NF." Could you tell us exactly what this acronym stands for?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but as it's a narrow column, the "I" went missing, was lost. It's "ID/NF," which means the mortal remains went missing, ID, with the DNA analysis method being applied; however the family did not accept the identification. So that actually means identified, not accepted, so it should be "ID," it should be "ID."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. So we should read "ID/NF" instead of "D/NF." It's a printing error, obviously.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
