utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying the family did not accept the identification, but for what reason? They were challenging the reliability of the DNA analysis, or was it on just principles that they rejected the identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the 193 persons whose mortal remains were identified, we have 3 persons or, rather, 3 cases in which the mortal remains were identified by the DNA analysis method, but their families refused to accept that identification, probably for psychological reasons. Probably the reasons were psychological, for the fact that the family members did not wish to accept that, because they couldn't accept the fact that their nearest and dearest were had been killed and that that was the end of it, that they had no further hope and could not expect that they might be alive somewhere. So I assume that that was the reason for which they refused to accept the results of the identification process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Talking to the psychologists now, as far as you know, did the authorities set up any psychological support units or was nothing done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of every process of identification for the mortal remains, psychologists and psychiatrists are always present; and they are there to provide assistance to families in that specific situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But then there are interviews and people are helped psychologically when they're finally told that the hope they had to find their missing relative is gone. With the reality of DNA analysis, they can no longer hope for this person to still be alive, and then is there interviews or is there any psychological support that is provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, the process of identification in the Republic of Croatia is attended by experts for social and psychological assistance to the families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now, some clarifications on your acronyms, please. In the column called "Circumstances," what exactly does "MG" mean?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: "Mass Grave," "Masovna Grobnica."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. What about "PG"?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Individual grave, "Pojedinacna Grobnica."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: "PO"?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Mortal remains, "Posnartne [phoen] Ostaci."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And "VNG"?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Vukovar New Cemetery, "Vukovar Novo Groblje."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. All in all, how many people listed in appendix 3 of the indictment can be found on the list of people identified in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you please now quickly move to document 7375. It's the next document in the binder. Is this the list of the 190 persons you mentioned who were identified and who are also in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: We know that in Ovcara, 193 bodies were identified. You're telling us that 190 people are on the annex 3 list that is joined to the indictment. I infer from this that three people were identified in Ovcara, but are not on the annex 3 list in the indictment. Now, could you tell us whether document 7379 gives us a list of these three missing people?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's be very clear about this. Those three people in question, could they be the three people for which the families did not want to accept the identification made through DNA analysis or is it three other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is three completely different persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we have a person called Bukvic, Bordaj [phoen]; Omerovic, Mufat [phoen]; and Vazic, Mikajlo [phoen]. If I understand you well, these three are not in the list in annex 3. Does this mean that the Prosecutor just neglected to add them or is it three other people that ended up there for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These three people were not on the list for another reason, a different reason, and that reason was this: In the questionnaires, describing the circumstances of their disappearance, no mention is made of the fact that they were last seen in the Vukovar Hospital. It doesn't say that. So under "Description of circumstances," all that is recorded is, in general terms, that they disappeared in Vukovar; and that's the reason why, when the list was compiled, we did not know that it was possible that the three people mentioned might be found at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we assume that 200 people left the hospital building to be driven or taken to the execution site, then these would be included in these 200 people. That's the first assumption that comes to mind. However, another assumption could be explored. These three would not be in the hospital building, were killed or executed somewhere else, we have no idea where, and were buried there. So as far as you're concerned, which one is the right assumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very difficult for me to speculate, and I think that the proper answer would be that their families, when they tabled their request for the tracing process to be put into practice, did not know the specific circumstances of their disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This question was very relevant indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Out of the 265 persons listed at annex 3 of the indictment, 190 are amongst those who were identified at Ovcara. What information do you have about the 75 other persons listed at annex 3 of the indictment and who are not amongst the bodies found at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: A portion of them, that is to say, 57 of them, are still listed as missing. And their fate has not been established, so they are not amongst the identified persons found. The other two people, two more people, Damir Kiralj [phoen] and Zvonko Mikolic were found in the territory of the Republic of Serbia; and their mortal remains was taken over by the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons from the Republic of Serbia. They were identified in the Republic of Croatia and handed over to their families. Sixteen persons who are listed in annex 3 of the indictment were found and exhumed in other mass graves or individual graves on the territory of Vukovar. Thirteen of them, of that number, were found at the Novo Groblje, New Cemetery, in Vukovar. Two were found in individual graves in the area of Velepromet in Vukovar; and one person, I think, was found in a mass grave at the Lovas farm not far from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I've almost completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you've almost run out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm aware of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What about Velepromet? 65 ter number 7381. You were asked by the Prosecution to analyse annex 4 of the indictment. What are your conclusions about the list of victims of Velepromet to be found at annex 4 of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: These six persons listed in annex 4 to the indictment were buried in the territory of Velepromet, and they were exhumed in the beginning of December 1991 by the representatives of the then-authorities of the occupied area; and they were transferred to Vukovar, the New Cemetery, where they were reburied, and then we exhumed them in 1998. All of the six were identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But these six persons had been killed in December 1991; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the information about the circumstances of their disappearance or forcible removal, they were forcibly removed on the 19th of November, 1991. According to the documentation that the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons received from the Republic of Serbia, it transpires that the mortal remains of these six persons had been found in the mass grave in Velepromet and had been exhumed from there in December 1991. They were examined and then reburied at the New Cemetery in Vukovar as "unidentified."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the most likely explanation is the following: They were captured on the 19th of November, 1991. They were executed at some point. We don't know exactly when. They were buried. Once again, we don't know exactly when. They were exhumed in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very quickly, Witness, could you please have a look at the six following documents bearing 65 ter numbers 2017, 2004, 2010, 2009, 2008 and 2016. Could you confirm that these are missing persons questionnaires relating to the six victims?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very quickly, Your Honour, the same question about the missing persons questionnaires related to Ovcara, we have two documents that were already on the 65 ter lists. All the other documents in binder 2 are not -- have not been translated, except for 389.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you have a look at the last two documents of binder 1 and confirm that these are, indeed, missing persons questionnaires?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Correct, these are questionnaires for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you turn to binder 2, to the red binder, and have a look at all the documents except the last two documents. 7382 -- this is going to be a long list, but I need to identify these documents specifically -- 7383, 7384 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Judges, so that Mr. Dutertre doesn’t kill us by reading all these figures. I have no objection to this entire binder being admitted into evidence. He will kill us with these figures, my head is already spinning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to Mr. Seselj for his cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no challenge from the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These documents have been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you confirm that these are official missing persons questionnaires you're very familiar with?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are missing person questionnaires that I am familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Unless I'm mistaken, I believe the last 65 ter number is 7412.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Let me conclude by asking you how many prisoners were recorded on the territory of Croatia during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: In the Republic of Croatia, 7.666 persons had been taken prisoner during the war, related to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In your first binder, is document 7363 a document analysing the data related to these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What is the percentage of civilians amongst these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: There was 1.865 civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, I have no further questions. I wanted to tender all the 65 ter documents I've shown to the witness: 7278, 7413, 7414, 7357, 7360, 7362, 7369, 7373, 7374, 7375, 7363, 7381, 7379, and all the missing persons questionnaires, 2012, 2013, I'm certain about these two, 2017, 2004, 2010, 2009, 2008, 2016; and the rest of the questionnaires we reviewed quickly, thanks to the cooperation of Mr. Seselj. They are to be found in the second binder. I don't know if you want me to list all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Give us the first number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope they are classified in the numerical order. The first number is 7382, and the last number is 7412. And I'm going to make sure that the documents are to be found in numerical order, but I'll do that later. I would also like to ask for the admission of the other documents I was not able to show to the witness. They are mentioned in the report of the witness, and she submitted them as annexes to her report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will need to deliberate on these documents, but after having heard the cross-examination by Mr. Seselj, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 7389.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a document that has not been translated yet, but that could be given an MFI number?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7389.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7389. This is a document that has not as yet been translated. Mr. Registrar, can we have a MFI number for 7389, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit number P630. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecutor has completed his examination-in-chief. We are now going to give the floor to Mr. Seselj for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, when you were doing the statistical reviews of the missing detainees, exhumed and identified persons in the territory of Croatia, why did you do it according to the new administrative division of Croatia? Why didn't you do it according to the administrative division that existed in 1991, so that data would be easier to understand and comparison would be easier?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: All the information that our administration keeps are harmonised with the official administrative division in the Republic of Croatia. It's the current one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's the point of my question. Why did you harmonise it with the current administrative division? Why not the administrative division that applied during the war in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what to answer, except what I have already said; namely, that information is harmonised and has been harmonised with the current administrative borders, all the more so because data concerning missing persons was collected in 1994, when, for the most part, the current division into counties already applied, and data about exhumations and identifications that started in 1995 were also processed in keeping with the current administrative division in Croatia into counties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Dalj and Ilok, were they separate municipalities in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how would I know if you, as an expert, don't know?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I am not familiar with specific issues of local self-government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You reviewed data here about exhumed and identified persons in the Vukovar-Srem county, and according to my information, and I have been in prison for six years so my knowledge is limited, this county has a large number of municipalities within it.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Vukovar, Ilok, Dalj and many others, newly-created municipalities?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but as far as I know Dalj is not in the Vukovar-Srem county, it's in the Osijek-Baranja county.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But we just had it here in -- on the map as part of the Vukovar-Srem county.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: That was a map of grave locations, graves where Vukovar victims were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Concerning the Lovas farm, you said victims from Vukovar were found there, whereas we know that the victims are actually locals of Lovas. And in Belgrade, the trial is going on of the perpetrators of these crimes that forced the victims into minefields.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. You are speaking so fast that the interpreters don't have time to complete their translation, so please wait until the interpreters have completed their translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Lattanzi now gave you another question which is food for thought. Do you know that the victims in Lovas were Croats from Lovas that a paramilitary formation had forced into a minefield and they got killed there? The alleged perpetrators are on trial at this moment in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I know that in Lovas, the victims are locals of Lovas, indeed, and I know that as we speak, there is a trial going on in Belgrade for a war crime against the inhabitants of Lovas. However, we are talking about the mass grave at Lovas farm, not Lovas settlement. Lovas farm is an agricultural estate between Dalj and Borovo village, and on Lovas farm, in 2000 or 2001, a mass grave was found, out of which 24 victims were exhumed, and the mortal remains of 20 of them have been positively identified so far. All the 20 were persons who had been taken away on the 19th of November, 1991, from Borovo settlement. So these are two different events and two different locations, Lovas farm versus Lovas settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in Borovo settlement, a completely different military unit of the JNA operated, completely different to the one that operated in Vukovar? These units were divided into Operative Group South and Operative Group North; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Nowhere in my report do I deal with persons who were responsible for these crimes or who operated in certain parts of Vukovar town or in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not talking about persons. We're talking about military operations that had taken place, causing a certain number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: But I'm not dealing with military forces or paramilitary forces which were involved in the events in the area of Vukovar in 1991. Therefore, I'm not familiar with the subject, it's not the subject of my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I fully understand what you are telling us. But beyond that, killings took place; and I'm discovering now that there were 24 bodies, 20 of whom were identified, that came from the village of Borovo. It's a village we've been told about earlier. They were executed on the 19th of November, 1991, and this is a key date because it's a date we've already heard mentioned in relation to other locations. But beyond that, the relatives of these casualties may have turned to your administration or the relevant administration. Why all this happened, did that happen as part of an overall plan, because, you see, relatives, families, are entitled to receive answers to such questions, or is this the result of the unregulated activities of units that were completely out of control? Did these events take place on those dates by pure chance? Is it something that is of interest to people in Croatia or is it something that no one is really interested in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my report, data is shown on 14 mass graves in the area of the Danube Valley in Croatia, where Vukovar victims were found. Part of these graves -- that is, most of those graves were made at the same time as the mass grave in Ovcara. So these are the facts that I can talk about at this time. Specific military units that acted in specific areas are something I am not familiar with. But the fact is that most of the mass graves containing Vukovar victims, such as Ovcara, Dalj, Petrovci Brsadin, the Lovas farm, Negoslavci, most of them were created and contain victims who had been forcibly removed on the 19th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to these mass graves, if I, myself, had been on the spot when they were discovered and when the exhumations took place, I would have asked myself the question whether these graves had been dug with an excavator, with simple shovels, and so on and so forth. Were inquiries conducted into these matters to find out how these graves were dug? Was it done with a machine? If that's the case, then this excavator had to be nearby. So any investigation worth its salt would have uncovered what had really happened. To your knowledge, were any investigations conducted in relation to the 14 mass graves mentioned in your report, about the way these mass graves were dug up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think most of these graves -- this is really a technical issue; but I believe most of these 14 graves, the pits where mortal remains were found, were dug up by machines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but they had to come from somewhere, these machines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just used a term that I have never heard before, neither in administrative nor geographic terms. You said "Croatian Podunavlje," Danube Valley.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, the unified term encompassing Baranja, Western Srem, and Eastern Slavonia, so that is the part of the Republic of Croatia along the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So these 14 graves relate also to graves found in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The victims from Vukovar were not found in any of the mass graves in the area of Baranja. In the table attached to the map, there is indication of exact locations of all mass graves where victims from Vukovar were found, so this map shows exclusively those mass graves that contain victims from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In that case, the least we can say is you are inadequately using the term "Croatian Podunavlje." "Croatian Podunavlje" could mean an area that Croatians currently hold on the banks of the Danube. But if you exclude such a large, important area such as Baranja, because none of these 14 graves were there, then using this term, "Croatian Podunavlje," is inadequate to say the least. You can talk about graves found in Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem; correct? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that in this specific case, a more accurate definition would be that graves were found in the Vukovar-Srem county and Osijek-Baranja county.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But these two counties did not exist in 1991. I, therefore, conclude that you deliberately used the new administrative division of Croatia to locate these mass graves, so as to create confusion and so that all exhumed bodies could artificially be linked to the action of liberation of Vukovar in 1991, in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. There's no point in all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the question is interesting, indeed. But in November and December of 1991, there was a specific administrative division in place. It was the time of the former Yugoslavia. You are describing a number of regions in your report, and these regions, they were established after the independence of Croatia. As part of this work you conducted, why did you make no reference to the regions as they existed, legally speaking, at the time? You're not responsible for all this, but why don't you do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The process of exhumation of mass and individual graves in the territory of the Croatian Podunavlje area was intensified in 1998, after the establishment of the full sovereignty of the Republic of Croatia over the area. At the time when the exhumation processes began in the area, the administrative setup prevailed, which is the one that I showed in my data, and that is how all the data and information and records are kept, on that basis. However, for each mass grave in which victims from Vukovar were found, data was listed which enable its very precise location, which enable us to locate it very precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, you say here that 2.017 victims were exhumed in the Vukovar-Srem county area. That's right, isn't it? Now, all these 2.017 victims, do you link them up to the second half of November 1991? To give you a bit more manoeuvring space, let me put it that way, so not to focus on one day, the 17th, 18th, 19th or 20th of November. Now, all of these victims, did they die in the second half of November?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: No. The data on the 2.017 exhumed persons relate to the occupied parts of the Vukovar-Srem county or, according to the previous system, it was the former Vukovar municipality and occupied parts of the former municipality of Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who occupied that area, who did the occupying?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, those areas were occupied by the Yugoslav People's Army and its associated paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How could the Yugoslav People's Army occupy parts of Yugoslavia itself? Tell me that.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The Croatian Sabor Assembly, on the 8th of October, 1991, passed a constitutional decision on the cessation of all state legal ties to the former republics which made up Yugoslavia, and with Yugoslavia as a whole, and this was on the 8th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: With respect to the constitutional role --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, there must be a mistake. It's October 8, 1991, not 1990. What you say is very important, Witness. Through its decision of October 8, 1991, Sabor said that it cut any links with Yugoslavia. This was the -- you know everything that happened. And then there was international recognition that occurred with the UN and with other states, which recognised, despite the fact that on October 8th, the -- despite that this was said by the Croatian Parliament, on October 8, you know -- let me repeat my question. Despite the fact that the Sabor, on October 8, 1991, declared that all links with the former Yugoslavia were cut off, the former Yugoslavia had a legal army at the time, and it was the JNA? Was that the fact, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not an expert in this area for me to be able to give a proper answer to this very complex question which has its legal and historical implications, but the fact remains that the Croatian Sabor or Assembly, on the basis of a decision made by the citizens of the Republic of Croatia, passed a referendum on the 8th of October, 1991, did pass the decision to put a stop to all social and legal links and connections. But unfortunately I'm not in a position to answer your question, because I'm not a professional in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's assume, and it's just an assumption, let's assume that today in Croatia a region would declare itself autonomous, that this municipality would declare itself autonomous. So today, the army in force would be the Army of the Republic of Croatia in this area, it would still be that army that would be in that region; do you agree with this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. However, I really am not a lawyer, nor am I a political science specialist, and this enters the realm of my own personal positions, which I don't think is suitable for the subject matter that I have been called in to testify about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, nonetheless, in my estimation, you are a highly-intelligent and educated person. I can see that you are a psychology graduate, so you must be fully conscious of the fact that from the aspects of the constitutional role of the Yugoslav People's Army, the Croatian Sabor, on the 8th of October, could have only passed a decision to prevent the falling of leaves in autumn, because in autumn leaves do fall; so the Croatian Sabor had no other authorisation and powers to discuss the constitutional role of the Yugoslav People's Army; isn't that right? So as an intelligent or educated person, I'm sure you'll realise that, although you're not a lawyer by profession, but you know that full well; right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your compliments. However, these questions rank among the questions of personal positions being put forward, and therefore, independently of my degree of education, I cannot, before this august Trial Chamber and in such a serious situation, present my own views and attitude on something that I'm not an expert in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, when somebody engaged you as an expert, that is to say, the OTP of The Hague Tribunal, I assume that they told you that as an expert, in the courtroom you must be completely unbiased; so your own political passions and ideological convictions must be laid aside and you must only speak the language of facts. And in that respect, you should not speak about parts of occupied Croatia, but on the situation as it existed, the facts as they existed; that is, the existence of the RSK, and in the civil war that was waged, the attempt by the Yugoslav People's Army to repress the Croatian separatist rebellion, to make a long story short.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: In this question, just like in the previous questions, we see observations made which have both legal and political repercussions; so I really cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well, fine. Now, for me not to have to oppose you and put opposing thesis, that Croatia occupied the Republic of Serbian Krajina in 1995 and that that temporary occupation is still ongoing today, and so that you can avoid -- would you avoid talking about temporarily-occupied territory, and let's stick to the facts in your expert report . Do you agree with that; can we strike a bargain there?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that I should respond to questions that relate to my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, you said that in the Vukovar-Srem county, a total of 2.017 persons were exhumed or, rather, victims were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Those were victims who had died over a longer period of time, not just those several days at the end of November 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, the period is a broader one, and I think that the first victims fell at the end of August or the beginning of September 1991. The largest number of victims took place on the 18th, the 19th and 20th of November, 1991, as we said. However, there were victims before, that is to say at the very beginning of 1992. So from August 1991 right through to the beginning of January and February of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, among those 2.017 victims, almost 1.000 people were exhumed in the Vukovar grave, 900 odd, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: 938 individuals were exhumed at the new grave in Vukovar, to be exact; so that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they were people that were buried according to all the rules and regulations and whom the Yugoslav People's Army buried, having sanitised the terrain and collected up bodies temporarily buried in various parts of Vukovar, and even temporary graves in town parks which the Croatian soldiers set up to bury those who fell victim within their own ranks; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The grave at Novo Groblje in Vukovar, the New Cemetery in Vukovar, is a locality where the mortal remains were buried of persons who had died under different circumstances. Part of those individuals really did die before the 18th or 19th or 20th of November, 1991; and they were temporarily buried. Then they were exhumed and transferred to the New Cemetery at Vukovar. Now, some of the people lost their lives 17 years ago, before those dates, but then again a portion of the people found at the New Cemetery in Vukovar lost their lives after the 20th of November, and they were temporarily -- or part of them were temporarily buried in what we term primary grave-sites, just like the grave-site at Velepromet that we spoke about earlier on, then the Petrovacki Atar [phoen] grave-site, the fairground and Grbica Sesta [phoen] graveyards. So they were temporary grave-sites. In 1991, an expert team led by Dr. Stankovic from the Medical Military Academy, processed those mortal remains. They were therefore exhumed from those primary grave sites and transferred to the New Cemetery in Vukovar, and the people who were buried at the New Cemetery in Vukovar, it was the Commission for Tracing Missing Persons from the Republic of Serbia that sent us the identification protocols.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the difficulty that any reasonable Judge may have when dealing with your report is the following: Notably regarding this 2.017 bodies exhumed, this is the following problems that a Judge may run into, and you've already answered a number of these questions: We need to know when these people were killed. You said that as far as you're concerned, some people were killed in 1991. You mentioned July, August, so we have one first difficulty here. The second difficulty, Vukovar. We know that the town was shelled by the JNA, that combat occurred, that Croat soldiers were killed in these combats, and compounded difficulty. We need to know whether these people that were killed were killed in combat and then buried later on. We need to know, among those people, which ones were the civilians and which ones were military. And there is another difficulty, a third one. When Vukovar is taken, prisoners are made; and we need to know what happens afterwards, why some POWs are actually killed. This has to do with the Ovcara farm, notably. Then you seem to have said that after November 1991, other people were killed, but we don't know the circumstances surrounding their death. Because of all this, this figure of 2.017 for the Vukovar-Srem region seems to hide very different situations, in terms of time, with -- in terms also of repercussions. We need to know who was in the armed forces, who was a civilian, and so forth and so on. Was this dealt with in the answers that you gave to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that 2.017 persons, who were exhumed in the Vukovar-Srem county area, were individuals who had fallen casualty between the end of August 1991 to the beginning of 1992. It is also true and correct that they lost their lives in different situations and under different circumstances. When I was answering a previous question, I stressed that these 2.017 exhumed victims were exhumed from 52 mass grave-sites and a series of individual graves as well. Now, each of these mass graves, the way in which they came into being, it was specific and would require an exact description of the circumstances in which these people lost their lives. Now, the fact remains that among the exhumed persons, specifically in Vukovar at the New Cemetery there, which is something that Mr. Seselj brought up a moment ago, there were persons who lost their lives due to shelling or were killed in other circumstances before the events of the 18th, 19th and 20th of November, 1991. So we have a very broad spectrum of circumstances and situations there, but most of the people who were found in the mass graves were individuals who were forcibly taken away, and the next fact about them that we know is the point at which they were found and exhumed from the mass graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question, please. You agree that all situations are always different, and this brings me back to the figure that struck me, the number of women killed throughout this period. There's more than 800 women killed. That's a very high number. It would have been quite interesting to know how many females were killed in Vukovar, as such, in the city of Vukovar, if women are gathered with children in a cellar, for example, and that a shell falls exactly there, because the Serbs saw some soldiers -- Croat soldiers passing by in that area and were aiming at these soldiers, and unfortunately hit the cellar where all these civilians were hiding, which is what we call collateral damage, then of course a number of women die in these kind of events. As you see, the situation is extremely complex. Was this dealt with by all those who were working in your office or those working for the Croatian organisations dealing with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but could you be more specific in asking your question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be more specific. We noted that more than 800 females were killed. So given this figure, backed by documents, the following question could be raised: We need to know -- we would like to know the circumstances surrounding the death of these females. One assumption could be that maybe a number of females were killed in Vukovar itself, in the city itself, because maybe they had gathered in a place that was shelled for some reason. So a shell fell, killed civilians, females, children, possibly Croat soldiers that were passing by, and that the place had been shelled because the Serb forces had seen Croat soldiers in that area; and that's why they targeted this place. Then these people are very hastily buried during the fighting, and then they are reburied in the New Cemetery. Now, the question that comes to mind is that the situation is very complex; and what I would like to know, talking to the expert, that you are, I would like to be whether at your level, at the level of all your colleagues working in Croatia, on the identification of all these casualties, whether people really understood the complexity of the situation regarding the circumstances surrounding the death of all these people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, we had in mind all the time that the situations were very complex. It is true, especially in the town of Vukovar, that some of the people, and that includes women, died as a result of shelling, destruction of their homes, houses, and that is indisputable. However, it is also a fact that in Vukovar, a certain number of women had been taken prisoner, and they are still listed as missing, whereas some of them were found in Ilok, Novi Sad and Belgrade. And according to the available documentation, their mortal remains had been taken out of the river, which shows that these women had been killed and thrown into the Danube. Another fact is that in other parts of the Republic of Croatia, but also in the Vukovar-Srem and Osijek-Baranja counties, some of the women were killed because they had failed to leave their homes earlier. They had stayed even after the JNA entered the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true, Ms. Bilic, that among these 936 persons exhumed from the Vukovar Cemetery, there was a large number of civilians who, in the course of war operations, died of natural causes; old age, disease perhaps, maybe hunger?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: As for the causes of death of persons exhumed and identified, I cannot speak in any qualified way. Professor Strinovic, who was here last week, was certainly more qualified to answer this question. However, it is a fact, and I'm repeating this, that among the people who are buried at the New Cemetery at Vukovar, and we see that both from the documentation received from the competent commission in Belgrade and other sources, some had certainly died before the events of the 18th, 19th and 20th November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since you are holding a high position in the Croatian authorities, in a ministry, you must know that in the war, civilians had died from natural causes at the same rate they would have died without a war, and even more so because the war brings psychological and other traumas that can accelerate death by natural causes; and it was not possible to bury them at the cemetery because of various military actions, sporadic shooting, shelling, et cetera; so they were buried in improvised graves, in parks and other locations, whereas the JNA, after military operations, conducted sanitization, collected bodies, exhumed bodies from such improvised graves, and reburied them properly. I emphasise "properly." But the competent authorities of Yugoslavia turned over to you all the necessary documentation about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't -- I'm not against this question, but could we please break it down into several statements, because it's too complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you understand Mr. Seselj's question? It's a very long question, long winding. He gave us a lot of information in this question, but can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood the question of Mr. Seselj, and I can try to answer. As Mr. Seselj said, in 1991 the representatives of the Military Medical Academy from Belgrade came to Vukovar, and in the area of Vukovar, a sanitization was conducted of mortal remains. On that occasion, in addition to the mortal remains found on the very surface, also exhumed were temporary graves Mr. Seselj referred to containing the remains of persons who, because of war, could not be buried in cemeteries. But also exhumed were primary graves containing the mortal remains of those who had been forcibly removed or captured and then killed. And all these mortal remains were transferred and reburied at the New Cemetery in Vukovar. They were designated, marked at the New Cemetery. However, it is a fact that among the mortal remains reburied at the cemetery in Vukovar, there were also remnants of medical supplies and debris; and there were cases also where mortal remains were not buried individually, but one on top of another. And it's also a fact that the markings on the crosses or tombs were not identical to the markings on the mortal remains. But to leave these details aside for the moment, the mortal remains were buried at the New Cemetery in Vukovar. And concerning them, the competent Commission from Belgrade did provide us with documentation. It is also a fact that the documentation on victims buried in 1991 at the New Cemetery at Vukovar was made available to the authorities in Croatia in 1996. In fact, the list was given in 1996, whereas the turnover of protocols was a process that took the next two years; and we received the last documentation on the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Obviously, the question wasn't complicated for you. It was only complicated for the Prosecutor, Mr. Dutertre, but let me -- he can handle only questions of a simple nature containing a few words, but you can handle longer and more complicated ones. You dealt here with the 200 bodies from Ovcara, out of which 7 were not -- have not yet been identified. Isn't it a bit strange that seven have still not been identified after twelve years? At least concerning Ovcara, we know that those are bodies from the Vukovar Hospital. A list was made, and Vesna Bosanac participated in the making of that list, although I was not allowed to discuss it with her here. And with all that information that you have, that these people had been at the Vukovar Hospital, that some of them had been, indeed, wounded, that some were bandaged up, and we know that from the post-mortems. They had bandages, although below the bandage there was no trace of wounds, and the Trial Chamber in Mrksic found that those were prisoners of war. And now, after all this time, seven have not yet been identified. Isn't that a bit odd?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: As I said, when I was answering the questions of the Prosecutor, and as we can see from the data attached to my report, with regard to three persons, at the time of the list --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's the three missing from 190 to 193. I'm speaking only about the last seven you haven't identified yet.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: It's possible that these seven persons, for the same reasons that I have given you concerning those three persons, were not included in the list of persons who had been forcibly removed from the Vukovar Hospital. It's possible that for the seven of them, the data available was not specific enough for them to be included in the list, or alternatively it's possible that their family members had not provided blood samples for DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we need to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just finish this, because it's logical to follow up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To pick up on the possibilities you mentioned, or alternatively those were foreign mercenaries and adventurers who had joined the ranks of the Croatian military and participated in the fighting in Vukovar and were captured as such. That possibility does exist, doesn't it; they are foreigners and that's why you can't identify them after so many years?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Calling for speculation. Objection. Calling for speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it can be an assumption you make. What do you have to answer to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons, where I work, deals with searching for missing persons primarily from the humanitarian point of view. If families had submitted requests for a search, the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons would have taken blood samples for DNA analysis and included these people in the list and tried to ascertain their fate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we know that some people went missing. We know that some families got in touch with you. Seven persons remain unidentified. If you take samples of hair, blood samples of people looking for a relative, and if you conduct a DNA analysis, comparison, between these people and the seven unidentified bodies, you should be able to ascertain whether these seven people are amongst the missing persons. But since we do not know, as of today, where these seven people come from, it may very well be that some of them were foreigners, because, you see, when I had a look at your tables, I was quite astonished to see that there were victims from various nationalities. There were Germans, Ukrainians, and so on and so forth. So could it be that some of these seven are foreigners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's true and it's a fact that in my report, there is information about the ethnicity of both missing persons and identified persons; but it is a peculiarity of especially Vukovar and the surrounding area, that is, the former municipalities of Vukovar, Osijek, Bela Manastir and Vinkovci, that this is an area inhabited by a large number of ethnicities: Ruthenians, Hungarians, Romanians, Czechs and others. So in this case, these are ethnic communities living in the territory of the Republic of Croatia who were also victimised alongside Croats. There were also among victims members of these ethnic communities that were exposed to suffering. That is about ethnicity. Now, about these seven persons exhumed at Ovcara who have not been identified yet, I repeat it is my opinion that the answer probably lies in the fact that the families of these persons did not have accurate data on the location where the missing persons had been seen the last time. They did not know that they had last been seen precisely at the Vukovar Hospital, and it is possible that these are persons for whom not enough samples have been collected to enable DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And maybe they are simply Kurds or similar mercenaries, because there have been such cases. Who knows who they are. Germans from Germany came, not local Germans. Poles from Poland came. Other foreigners came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One quick question about these seven individuals. Is it the case that not a single item of clothing was found? Was everything destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I'm not able to give you such specific data. I don't know whether Professor Strinovic could provide a better answer to the question, perhaps, than me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We really need to break now. It's 10 past 12.00. We'll resume at half past 12.00 for 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, according to our calculations, you've used 32 minutes. You have 58 minutes left. You won't be able to complete your cross-examination today, since we have to stop at a quarter past 1.00. We'll need to proceed with the testimony of the witness tomorrow, unless you manage to complete your cross-examination within the 50 minutes we have left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have to go on tomorrow, Mr. President, because I am sure you'll have additional questions, and I don't think we'll be able to get through it today. I'll need the full hour that's left to us today, so that will probably take longer overall, and I'm sure Ms. Bilic won't find it hard to come back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Anyway, Ms. Bilic, when you, as far as I understood it, for the first time in your life were given the assignment to write an expert report for a court of law, that's the first time you've been asked to do anything like that; right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, this is the first time that I have written a report for a court of law, the first time that I'm doing an expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Wasn't it a little strange that you were asked to write an expert report without being provided with the title and heading of that expert report, that is to say, succinctly your assignment defined? You received a list of questions from Ms. Christine Dahl to which she wanted your response, but you never actually got the subject of your expert report formulated in the form of a heading or title. Didn't you find that a little strange?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't find it strange, to be quite frank. I didn't pay any attention to the fact that this subject, specified subject, was lacking, since the specific questions that I was asked and was asked to incorporate in my report actually referred to my field of work and expertise. And I've already said the uniform title could be the process of seeking detainees and missing persons in the Republic of Croatia. That could be the working title.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that would then be an expert report, were it that the Republic of Croatia was being tried here, so you should analyse the process which the authorities there were putting into practice. However, the subject matter here is far broader, and for that it is indispensable to address such matters as the process of determining the number of missing persons in the first place during the war and the war activities of 1991 up until 1995, regardless of who deals with subject matter of that kind within national borders. And you only have one source, and they are data and information from the corresponding ministry of the Republic of Croatia; there was no other source that you used in writing your report. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The title of the report, "The process for tracing missing persons in Croatia," would be quite sufficient and would be comprehensive for information and data that I present in my report. The process in which missing persons were traced includes the recording and listing of missing persons; and so it begins with a portion that we call recording and listing the names of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you conducted that listing and those records in relations of the citizens that recognise you as their authority, the Croatian powers and authorities, but not with the others; right?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: No, that is not right. The listing of missing persons was done, and all the families, citizens of the Republic of Croatia who have a family member who is missing, and the fact that he's missing was linked to the war events, did have the possibility and still do, in fact, have the possibility of tabling a request for tracing that person. And the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons would be in charge of that, taking in their requests and acting upon them. And as I describe in my report, the information and data pertaining to missing persons in the Republic of Croatia were collected in two stages, two general stages. First of all, there was the activity to renew the request for missing person search that was conducted in 1994; and the second stage was at the initiative of the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons on the basis of bilateral agreements with the representatives of the Republic of Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and in cooperation with the International Red Cross Committee, and they collected data and information pertaining to all missing persons whose families had responded to the drive and formulated a request for the search process to begin. So in that data-gathering process, it was the International Committee of the Red Cross that took part, and in the specific action implemented on the ground, it was the National Red Cross Society and Red Crescent -- or, rather, Red Cross Society, first of all of Yugoslavian -- Serbian and Bosnia and Herzegovina which took part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What about the publication of International Red Cross Committee that was published on missing persons and detainees on the territory of the former Yugoslavia; did you have that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, no. However, the International Committee of the Red Cross did publish a list of missing persons on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It also published a list of missing persons in Kosovo. And finally, in February 2007, a book was published containing a list of missing persons on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. This book was published by the International Red Cross Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How far do your -- does your information differ from the facts and figures found in that particular book, in that publication?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The information that the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons has have been almost totally dovetailed with the information contained in the book "Missing Persons in the Territory of the Republic of Croatia," which was published by the International Red Cross Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you able to establish how many people were killed on the territory of the Republic of Yugoslavia, the former federal unit of Yugoslavia, from 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons does not keep records of persons killed or, rather, the fatalities, so that I am not in a position to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But Ivan Grujic bandies a figure of about 11.000 fatalities; right? Have you heard about that? No?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I certainly have heard of that. That piece of information is something I'm aware of. But as an expert witness, I've been called here to discuss missing persons, exhumated, and identified persons and persons who were freed and then exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, when you wrote your expert report, you knew that you had to be unbiased and objective. Why didn't you seek information from the government of the RSK in exile, whose seat is in Belgrade, and from the nongovernmental organisation called Veritas, which is led by Savo Strbac, because they have the number of disappeared Serbs, missing Serbs, that you don't have and that were not dealt with by the International Red Cross either.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons, when establishing their list of missing persons, stem from --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. You're now defending the administration. I'm asking you, personally, and as an expert, because when you accepted to be an expert witness of the International Tribunal, you should have left your function aside that you hold in the administration -- Croatian Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons. You're a expert witness of the International Tribunal, and you must seek alternative sources of information and data which might be opposed to the ones you have. So you must be unbiased and set your personal feelings aside. So that's the substance of my question.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: The Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons, let me repeat once again, when compiling its list of missing persons and its records of missing persons, not in a single case was guided by the information from nongovernmental organisations, but by standards and criteria applied by the International Red Cross Committee, which stem from the fact that for each missing person, there must be somebody seeking that person, a family member who wants to find the person; and that is how the list of missing persons was set up in Croatia, regardless of their origins, ethnicity, religion, or the circumstances of their disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But most of the expelled Serbs from the RSK --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. Witness, I do not want to challenge your independence. You're an expert witness, and as such, you are independent. But I would like to know the following: When you drafted your report, did you submit it to a higher-up in your administration in Croatia or did you draft a report and immediately send it to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I compiled the report and sent it directly to the OTP of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, no one controlled your report; you drafted your report independently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I compiled it fully independently, and the report describes my methodology and the results on the basis of official records kept by the institution in which I am employed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I had to check this with you. We are dealing with the collateral issue of Serb victims. It's a question I raised myself earlier. I did not wait for Mr. Seselj to do so. I raised it first, when I dealt with the 184 Serbs who were killed. And I have a question about this. As part of the mandate that was yours, you were dealing with Croats who had been killed and who had gone missing. But notwithstanding that fact, as an expert, as somebody interested in everything, wouldn't it have been natural for you to wonder what happened on the other side, to wonder how many Serbs were taken prisoner in the Republic of Croatia, how many were killed, how many went missing? Wouldn't an independent expert have naturally conducted such an inquiry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, that's how I worked. I worked that way personally, and that's how the institution in which I'm employed works too. As I've already said, in 1994 there was a drive to gather information about missing persons, and the information gathered was mostly information about Croatian missing persons. But in 1991 and 1992, it was mostly ethnic Croats that fell casualty. Now, in 1995, we had Operations Flash and Storm take place, in which a certain number of citizens of the Republic of Croatia went missing, mostly of Serb ethnicity. It was precisely at the initiative of the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons, the institution of which I'm a staff member, in July 2000. At negotiations held in Zagreb, it was agreed and planned to have an action to gather information about missing persons in the Flash and Storm operations, and all persons who went missing and whose families had not put in a request for tracing the missing person. This drive was, as I said, initiated by the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons on the basis of bilateral negotiations, and in the process of collecting information, we had the International Red Cross Committee taking part as a completely unbiased organisation with the greatest possible humanitarian respect and esteem, as did the Red Cross societies of Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, since some of the families of the missing persons had spent time and were still living on the territory of those states. Now, bearing in mind, therefore, the displacement of families in general, this drive went on from 2002 up until 2006, and that drive at that point in time came up with a number of 1.110 missing persons, of which persons of Serb ethnicity made up the majority. The Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons, first of all through the process of identifying the mortal remains of these individuals, was able to establish the fate of a portion of these people. So when the report was compiled, which I sent to the OTP of the Tribunal, the number of missing persons from the drives I mentioned amounted to 874. What I'd like to add is this: In order to gain a comprehensive and objective picture, the criteria of data-gathering and the methodology applied to data-gathering were identical in the drive conducted in 1994 as they were in this latest drive of information-gathering; and so on the basis of that, the number established was 874 persons as of the 1st of July, 2008, which I also describe in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Seselj, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Bilic, what was the total number of camps for Serb detainees in Croatia, whether they were civilians or prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer to that question, I'm afraid. All I know is that there were, I think, two accommodation premises for prisoners of war, two facilities where the prisoners of war were put up. As to the other persons, they were in detention and in prisons; but the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons does not keep any official records of persons who were within the authorities of the Croatian authorities linked to the war events, so I can't give you a precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I notice that places where Croatian prisoners of war, i.e., referred to with camps, "logor," and where the Serbs were kept, you refer to them as accommodation sites for spending the night. So these just spend time spending the night, whereas you use the word "logor" or "camp" to associate us in our minds with the German concentration camps and so on?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I did not succumb to any propaganda when I compiled my report. In my report, there's no mention -- I don't use the word "konaciste" or accommodation for the night for prisoners of war. I used terms that are in official use in the Republic of Croatia and in the respective services.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you introduced this word "konaciste" quite recently as being "lodgings." "Konaciste" is an ancient Serb word that Croats use, too, meaning "quarters," but quarters and lodging for the night, somewhere you go to spend the night. That's what "konaciste" means, whereas where prisoners of war are held, the term there is "camp" that is used both by Serbs and Croats. And you use it, too, when you refer to places where the Croatian prisoners were kept. So why the difference? I understand that it's in official use, but as an expert witness, you should have raised yourself above that and used the same terminology, the same yardstick, for both the Croatian and Serb sides.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: As I said, nowhere in the report did I mention or use that word for one night lodging, but I am now using the terms officially accepted in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you based your report exclusively on the official data of the Croatian state, and the Croatian state is interested in Croat detainees in Serb or Muslim hands. But what Croats are holding in their hands, including Muslims whom you transported from Bosnia deep into Croatia, they are not interested. According to the government of the Serbian Krajina in exile and their prime minister, Mr. Buha, in the area of Croatia there were 221 camps detaining Serbs. Those are also the figures of the Veritas nongovernmental organisation headed by Mr. Strbac, 221 camps holding Serb prisoners. And you know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: I cannot speak of the things that I do not know. Detention centres and prisons in Croatia are within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But as an expert of an international court, you shouldn't have used only what is available to your ministry. You should have researched the whole phenomenon. As an expert of the International Court, you should be indifference whether the prisoners are Croats or Serbs. You have to establish the exact figures for both ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think the witness said what she knew and didn't know. We could keep on with this for hours, but it's pointless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your position. I discover that there is a government of the Serbian Krajina in exile in Belgrade, that's news to me; and I'm also discovering, that's according to Mr. Seselj, that in Croatia at the time, there would have been 221 detention camps where Serbs were detained. Line 15, page 88. So we could infer from this that there were some hundreds of Serbs detained there. Your department is competent to deal with missing persons, so I would like to know whether your department is sometimes -- sometimes gets inquiries by Serbian families looking for their own relatives who disappeared, or whether this is channeled through another department.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons searches for all missing citizens of the Republic of Croatia who had gone missing as a result of the war; and within the administration, requests have been made to search for 874 persons; that is, 874 requests are outstanding, mainly related to Flash and Storm operations, most of them Serbs; and 64 requests, again mainly Serbs, are outstanding. These persons, these families, through the mediation of the ICRC, addressed their administration, filed their requests for such; and it is precisely the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons that deals with these requests and searches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me assume a very theoretical case, but we'll use this as an example. Let's imagine we have a Serb who at the time was working in Germany, in 1991 he was working in Germany. Say that he volunteered to go fight in Croatia. This person might have a Serbian citizenship or maybe German citizenship. And let's say that he goes missing and no one has heard from him since then. I would like to know whether your department could receive an inquiry on this person, even though he is not a Croat national.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're talking about a citizen of the Republic of Serbia, in that case it's necessary to address the competent service of Serbia that would record that person as missing; and they would also need to be reported to the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But why go through the ICRC? Why is it that the family can't directly inquire with the competent authorities? Why is there a need for this to be channeled through the ICRC? In my assumption, you know, this Serb who was working in Germany and who went missing, I would like to know whether his relatives, maybe his mother, brother, sister, you know, wouldn't just directly write to your department or to the Serbian authorities in order to get information on this missing person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, they can directly address the authorities. But in this specific case, if a citizen of Serbia is concerned, the competent institution they should address would be the Commission for Missing Persons for the Government of the Republic of Serbia; and if it's a citizen of Croatia, the competent institution would be the Administration for Detainees and Missing Persons. I mentioned the ICRC because they have a network of branch offices throughout the world, and families sometimes find it easier and more practical to file their requests for tracing with the ICRC, who would distribute the request and send a query to the competent service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that in 135 mass graves in the territory of Croatia, Serb victims have been exhumed? The exact figure is 135.

utterances.speaker: VISNJA BILIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware that Serb victims have been exhumed out of 135 mass graves in the territory of Croatia, but I do know that out of 3.100 identified persons in the organisation of our administration, mortal remains of 184 Serb persons have been identified up to the date of the last update of my report. Now, that number is certainly higher, but at that moment the number of identified Serbs was 184.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: During the war, did you live in Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one point. Regarding these figures, it would be very useful if Mr. Seselj could give us documents or could give our witness documents to know exactly what she's talking about, because we're talking in a very general fashion about figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, you are stating facts, and I'm sure that this is backed by documents that you have. And so in order to, you know, back your question, please tell us where you obtained this information and which document it comes from. Otherwise, you know, you could have made it up, and Judges could think that you've made it up and the Prosecutor could think that you've made it up. So please give us references. Earlier, you were saying that there were 135 mass graves. You must have something to back this information. Tell us where you obtained this information. Tell us that the report was drafted maybe by the government of the Krajina, the exiled government, published in such year, talking about this. Give us some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution would like to have the list of the documents that Mr. Seselj is using in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but that's another kettle of fish, if I can say so. So just to add some credibility to what you're asserting, please tell us where you got this information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, they ban all my contacts with my advisers and associates, and now they want documents from me. If I had contact with my associates, you would have all sorts of documents on your table this morning. But I have the data from the government of the Serbian Krajina in exile; and according to the data of the Veritas NGO in the area of the Serbian Krajina, that is, the formal Croat federal unit, a total of 6.744 Serbs were killed, and they have a list of names. I would have all that here if my communication hadn't been stopped. I only using, in cross-examination, the information I had received before in a preliminary way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I was hoping that we would have had a document translated into English, not in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Seselj is stating from -- and this is backed by a document that he has, and I have no reason to challenge this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have on the transcript that the Prosecution is against the use by Mr. Seselj of documents that he says he had even before he was banned from contacting with his associates, because he would have been in a position to disclose them in time to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this is on the transcript now. Mr. Seselj is stating that backed by an NGO, Veritas, that 6.044 Serbs were killed in Croatia. So is this true, is it false?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I have already expressed my reservation concerning records of missing persons, but I don't have the list in front of me, that list of 6.744 persons who allegedly were killed in the Republic of Croatia. And without it, it would be frivolous of me to comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I have to point out that the Prosecution has chosen, as an expert in such a delicate issue, who is a civil servant of Croatia, one of the warring sides, and thus eliminated all semblance of objectiveness.
